name: Beard growth supplements (Beardalicious, etc.)

lead: Beard growth pills are commercial supplements, typically blends of vitamins such as biotin with herbal extracts, promoted to people who want fuller, thicker facial hair.

Marketing points to individual ingredients, and products vary. No clinical studies were found for the branded products, and reference sources report no randomized trials showing biotin helps hair in healthy people.

paras: They are taken as daily pills alongside normal beard care, usually for months, since hair grows slowly. Some people combine them with minoxidil or grooming routines.
US supplements can be sold without premarket approval, and analyses cited by Wikipedia have found mislabeling or undeclared drugs in some supplement categories. Biotin can interfere with lab tests.

The Role of Vitamins and Minerals in Hair Loss

angle.text: Vitamin and herbal blends are promoted as feeding follicles for a thicker-looking beard. The appearance benefit is a marketing claim; published trials of these branded products were not found.

lead: Beard growth supplements are branded oral products, usually vitamin and herbal blends such as biotin-based formulas, promoted for thicker, fuller facial hair. People take them hoping to fill in patchy areas and strengthen the beard they already have, as a lower-effort alternative to treatments such as minoxidil.[1][2]

Beard growth is driven mainly by hormones and genetics: Wikipedia reports that dihydrotestosterone stimulates follicles in the beard area, including after puberty, and that growth rate is inherited.[3] Marketing for supplements usually points to individual ingredients, especially biotin, which is involved in hair and nail biology.[4][5]

In the US these products are regulated as dietary supplements, which can carry structure/function claims with an FDA disclaimer but are not required to be approved before sale.[1] Reviews of biotin report limited evidence outside deficiency states and no randomized trials in healthy people.[4][5][6] No studies of specific branded beard supplements were found.

paras: Under the 1994 Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act, supplements are treated as food; disease claims are prohibited, and labels must state that structure/function claims are not FDA-evaluated.[1] The FDA can act on unsafe products after they are marketed.[1]

Wikipedia cites a 2015 New York Attorney General review that found only about 20 percent of tested herbal supplements contained the plants on the label (method disputed), and a study that found unlisted pharmaceuticals in 776 products sold from 2007 to 2016, mostly weight-loss or sexual-performance products.[1] These figures concern supplements broadly, not beard products specifically.

Wikipedia reports that DHT, made from testosterone, stimulates beard-area follicles and continues to act after puberty, and that beard growth rate is inherited.[3] Supplement makers generally describe their products as supporting hair rather than altering these drivers.
Biotin at 5 mg/day or more can interfere with thyroid and vitamin D immunoassays.[6]

A 2017 systematic review in Skin Appendage Disorders found 18 reported cases of biotin use for hair and nail changes, all in patients with an underlying condition affecting growth, all improving, and concluded evidence is limited and insufficient to support supplementation in healthy people.[4] A 2017 review in the Journal of Drugs in Dermatology likewise reported no randomized trials of biotin for hair quality or quantity in humans and described its popularity as exceeding the supporting evidence.[5] A 2019 review of vitamins and minerals in hair loss describes micronutrients as playing an important but not fully clear role in follicle function, notes that deficiency may be a modifiable risk factor, and calls for large placebo-controlled trials.[2]

No studies found of branded beard growth supplements. Related research is limited to reviews of biotin and micronutrients for scalp hair, mainly in people with deficiencies or hair loss conditions.[4][5][2]
